title: Carbon and Water Keep Going Around

scenes.tts: Scientists have measured carbon dioxide in the air on a Hawaiian volcano since nineteen fifty-eight. Each year it rises through winter and spring, then falls through summer. The whole record slowly climbs. Why? In Virginia, an oak pulls water from the soil. That water leaves as an invisible gas. Where do the carbon and the water go next?

scenes.tts: Carbon is in the sugar, fat and protein of every living thing. The carbon cycle is carbon moving among air, living things, ocean and soil. Photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide out of the air. Plants, algae and some bacteria use radiant energy to make sugar, called glucose, from carbon dioxide and water.

scenes.narration: Carbon is in the sugar, fat and protein of every living thing. The carbon cycle is carbon moving among air, living things, ocean and soil. Photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide out of the air. Plants, algae and some bacteria use radiant energy to make sugar, called glucose, from carbon dioxide and water.

scenes.tts: Three processes return carbon. Respiration is cells breaking down sugar and releasing carbon dioxide and water. Plants, animals and decomposers do it, day and night. Decomposition is bacteria and fungi breaking down dead organisms and returning carbon to air and soil. Combustion is burning. Burning coal, oil or natural gas releases carbon dioxide quickly.

Decomposition is bacteria and fungi breaking down dead organisms and returning carbon to air and soil. Combustion is burning. Burning coal, oil or natural gas releases carbon dioxide quickly.

scenes.tts: Water has its own cycle. Evaporation is liquid water changing into water vapor, a gas. Condensation is vapor cooling into droplets that form clouds. Precipitation is water falling as rain or snow. Infiltration is water soaking into the ground. Runoff is water flowing over land into streams. Transpiration is plants releasing water vapor from their leaves.
scenes.visual: water cycle around the oak, each process labelled as it is named

Precipitation is water falling as rain or snow. Infiltration is water soaking into the ground. Runoff is water flowing over land into streams. Transpiration is plants releasing water vapor from their leaves.

scenes.tts: The two cycles meet inside living things. Photosynthesis uses water and carbon dioxide together. In a dry summer, plants close the tiny openings in their leaves. That saves water, but less carbon dioxide gets in. A change in one cycle can change the other.
scenes.visual: leaf block takes water and carbon dioxide; openings close in a dry summer

scenes.tts: Back to the volcano. Most land plants are in the Northern Hemisphere. Each northern spring, leaves grow and photosynthesis speeds up. Each fall, photosynthesis slows and many trees drop their leaves, but respiration and decomposition keep going. Air at Mauna Loa mixes with air from across the north. So carbon dioxide falls each northern summer and rises each winter. Underneath, the record climbs, mostly from burning fossil fuels.
